data.name: Zaphiel
data.long_meaning: In Hebrew mythology, Zaphiel was considered the angel of the west. He led the armies of God against the forces of darkness. In Christian tradition, he is often identified with the archangel Michael, the prince of the heavenly host.
data.spiritual_meaning: Symbolizes strength, courage, and divine protection against darkness.
data.numerology_meaning: A harmonious and balanced soul, Zaphiel is a nurturer and a healer who seeks to bring peace and love to the world

in_latin.name: Zaphiel
in_latin.long_meaning: Zaphiel, Angelus Iustitiae, Visio Dei. Zaphiel est nomen angelorum qui apparuerunt Iesu in Monte Tabor. Visio Dei est apparitio divinitatis in forma angelorum.

in_english.name: Zaphiel
in_english.meaning: angel of justice, vision of God, heavenly messenger
in_english.long_meaning: Zaphiel is a name of an angel in the Book of Revelation, and is also used to refer to the angel who appeared to Jesus on Mount Tabor. The name Zaphiel is derived from the Hebrew words 'tzaphi' meaning 'angel' and 'El' meaning 'God'. The name is also associated with the concept of divine justice and the vision of God.

historical_references.reference: According to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian philosopher, Zaphiel is identified as the archangel who leads the celestial hierarchy and presides over the order of thrones.
historical_references.context: In the context of early Christian philosophy and angelology, Pseudo-Dionysius' works were highly influential in shaping the understanding of the celestial hierarchy and the roles of various angels, including Zaphiel.

historical_references.reference: In some Jewish and early Christian texts, Zophar and Zophiel are considered to be the same figure, with Zophar being the name used in Job and Zophiel being the angelic name. Zophar is depicted as a counselor to Job in the Book of Job, urging him to consider the divine justice behind his suffering.
historical_references.context: The name Zophar appears in the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament), while the angelic name Zophiel emerges in some Jewish and early Christian texts. The two names are believed to refer to the same figure, highlighting the evolving understanding of angels and their roles in religious traditions.
